cues.text: An Undefended Convent in a Time of War
By 1240, Emperor Frederick II , excommunicated and at open war with the papacy, had hired bands of Saracen mercenaries to campaign across central Italy on his behalf.
That September, one such company, advancing on Assisi, arrived first at the walls of San Damiano , the small, unfortified convent of Poor Clares just outside the town.
Carried to the Door with the Blessed Sacrament
Clare of Assisi , then forty-six and gravely ill, was confined to her bed when the terrified sisters ran to her.
By the earliest account of her life, drawn on for the testimony gathered at her canonization, she had herself carried to the convent entrance with the reserved Sacrament raised before her.
The Sacrament was kept, by the community's own custom, in a case of silver and ivory rather than the monstrance later artists would place in her hands.
She prayed: "Behold, my Lord, is it possible You want to deliver into the hands of pagans Your defenseless handmaids, whom I have taught out of love for You?
I pray You, Lord, protect these handmaids whom I cannot now save by myself."
A Retreat No One Could Explain
The soldiers who had already scaled the convent walls were, by the same early account, seized with sudden terror they could not themselves account for.
They fled back over the walls they had just climbed, leaving the community entirely unharmed; the wider imperial force is said to have turned away from Assisi itself the following day as well.
Testimony Given for Canonization
The episode entered the Church's official record when witnesses who had lived through it testified under oath during Clare's canonization process in 1253.
This occurred only two years after her death.
A Church otherwise cautious about embellished convent legend judged the testimony credible enough to include among the evidences of her sanctity.
Legacy
Clare died thirteen years after the attack.
In the centuries that followed, the episode became one of the most frequently painted scenes of her life.
Artists typically placed a monstrance in her hands, even though that particular vessel would not come into common use for another century after her death.
The story remains treasured less as a tale of miraculous rescue than as a witness to the same unshakeable Eucharistic confidence Clare had spent her whole religious life quietly practicing.
She trusted that the Lord she had given everything to serve could, in turn, be trusted completely with whatever she herself could no longer defend.
